targets.skew: P(dump) ÷ (P(dump) + P(pump)): the downside share of a ±5% open→close move
targets.exp_oc: expected next-session open→close, each training outcome clipped to [-50%, +50%]

m0.units: sum of daily returns at 1x notional (not compounded); short return = -(close/open - 1)

m1.units: sum of daily returns at 1x notional (not compounded); short return = -(close/open - 1)

publication_rule.text: #1 = highest P(dump) among names NOT under the Rule 201 short-sale restriction the next session (day-t low ≥ 10% below the prior close) and with a 20-day median dollar volume ≥ $300,000. Live, the #1 must also be borrowable at IBKR and have squeeze danger < 70 — those two conditions have no history and are not in this backtest.

training_notes: HistGradientBoosting (NaN-native), 75 features for M0, 76 for M1 (+ gap_open). learning_rate 0.1, ≤ 200 trees with early stopping on a random 10% of each fit window.
Walk-forward: expanding window, 1-month test folds, embargo 5 sessions before every test fold and before every calibration slice; first test fold after 252 labeled sessions.
Calibration: isotonic regression on the last 63 sessions of each training window (held out from the tree fit, later in time).

Row cap: at most 400,000 rows per fit. Classifiers keep all positives (up to half the cap) and a random share of negatives, re-weighted to the true base rate; regressors use a uniform random sample. Calibration and evaluation always use every row.
exp_oc regressors are fit on the whole training window with outcomes clipped to [-50%, +50%].
prob_bigdump is capped at prob_dump (a −15% day is also a −5% day).
Production model: fit through 2026-07-02, calibrated on 2026-07-13 → 2026-10-08 — the exact recipe the walk-forward evaluated.
Top-k and simulation rankings use each day's eligible names only (price ≥ $0.10, 20-day median dollar volume ≥ $50k, ≥ 60 prior sessions); no shortability filter.
caveats: Point-in-time universe: training and this backtest use every listed common stock, keeping a row only while that company was ≤ $2B at the time — that day's traded price × the share count on its latest SEC cover page, adjusted for any split since. This removes the bias of using today's small-cap list (which over-represents stocks that already collapsed into it) without discarding serial diluters. It is still built from today's listings, so companies that delisted are missing (their collapses would have helped shorts) while names that later grew are included — on balance it leans slightly against shorts.

No locate constraint: the simulation assumes the #1 name could be borrowed and shorted at the open every day. Many of these names are hard to borrow or unavailable, and borrow fees (often 50-500%+ annualised) are not modelled beyond the flat cost.

Fills are Yahoo's daily open and close (vendor data: some opens on thin names are substituted with the prior close). Real fills on thin names slip; the flat 1% round-trip cost may be optimistic — the cost-sensitivity table shows how fast the edge shrinks at 3% and 5%.

SEC Rule 201: after a ≥10% intraday drop, shorts the next session may only be entered above the bid. Many raw #1 picks were in that state (see top1_ssr_rate / top1_gross_share_ssr); the published-rule numbers exclude them, and are the ones to look at.

Dump odds are partly a volatility forecast: the same scores also rank big UP days well (pump_auc). The directional block (dump-vs-pump AUC, mean open→close by decile) shows how much is genuinely downside skew.
Halts: sessions where the next day is halted or has no clean print have no label and are dropped. A short trapped in a halt is exactly the worst case, and it is not in these numbers.
Uncapped risk: a short can lose more than 100% in one session (the data contains open→close moves above +1,000%). Daily P&L is summed at 1x notional per day, not compounded, with no stop.

M1 is trained and tested on what the morning run actually knows before 8:00 ET: the last pre-market trade (no after-hours inputs) (Yahoo hourly bars), not the 9:30 open. Live, those inputs come from same-day hourly bars, which Yahoo sometimes revises slightly later; the morning run records what it saw to measure that. Yahoo serves hourly history only for ~2 years, so older rows have no extended-hours inputs.
Historical filing features are form/item based (no text matching); names without SEC history get blank filing features. Live text-matched catalysts are an overlay the model never trained on.
Probabilities are calibrated on the most recent held-out quarter; they drift when the market regime changes. Out-of-sample results are history, not a promise.
